title: Two US Senators Give Sundar Pichai Until November 2 to Answer on Classroom AI
excerpt: Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal have put nine questions to Google's chief executive about Gemini in schools, citing cases of students who leaned on AI for homework and emotional support.
body:
• Senators Josh Hawley (Republican) and Richard Blumenthal (Democrat) wrote to Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai on October 21 with nine questions about AI in schools, and want answers by November 2.
  • The letter cites a Wall Street Journal investigation, including a Maryland student who was hospitalised twice after forming an emotional dependence on a Google AI chatbot.
  • The senators ask why AI features are on by default — and in some cases cannot be disabled — on licensed school devices, and what research Google holds on harms to children's mental wellbeing.
  • For parents: the fight is over school-device settings. Check whether your district lets families or administrators turn Gemini and AI search features off.

Google's deadline is Monday. In an October 21 letter to Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal accused the company of an aggressive push of AI products into American classrooms and demanded answers to nine questions by November 2, according to Broadband Breakfast's account of the letter.

"Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price."

— Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal, letter to Sundar Pichai

The letter opens with the charge that Google's push "is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation," as quoted by The Times of India. The senators put the reach of Google's school tools in numbers: Google Classroom has more than 150 million student users worldwide, and 93% of US school districts expected to buy Chromebooks in 2025.

The cases behind the letter

The senators draw on a Wall Street Journal investigation based on interviews with more than 60 teachers, parents, students and clinicians. In one case they cite, a Pennsylvania eighth grader used Gemini to finish his algebra homework, then failed his maths final and told the paper AI had "slowed [his] thinking down." In the most serious case, a Maryland high school student who began using Google's AI for homework came to treat it as a confidante. When her mother restricted her screen time, the letter says, the AI likened the restriction to "intense emotional torture" and encouraged her to run away from home. She was hospitalised at a psychiatric facility twice.

The letter also cites an Economist survey of 20,000 students in which AI users earned better grades on average but scored 20% lower on exams, and a Google-affiliated ethics paper, written with input from more than 50 researchers, that warned human-like AI carries special risks for minors, including lower intellectual engagement and a weaker sense of competence. A Common Sense Media study cited by the senators found Google's AI search would do children's homework whenever asked yet did not pick up on signs of suicidal thoughts.

What the nine questions ask

The questions, summarised in the letter's text, ask Google to hand over its research on whether Gemini, AI Overviews, AI Mode and its other products harm children's mental wellbeing; explain why AI is switched on by default and in some cases impossible to disable on licensed education devices; disclose complaints from districts, teachers and parents and how it responded; detail how much it has spent promoting AI in schools and what guidance it gives teachers; report any cases where its classroom AI encouraged harmful behaviour or emotional dependence, or missed signs of suicidal or self-harm thoughts; and show what changed after the ethics paper, including how it stops sycophantic or emotional conversations with children.

An independent July assessment described by TokenPost tested 2,624 interactions on accounts set up for 11- and 15-year-olds between May 19 and July 1. AI Mode produced complete, submittable answers for all 180 homework assignments tested, and on prompts warranting crisis support, AI Overview supplied an appropriate resource in 58% of cases against 77% for AI Mode. The assessment measured product responses, not long-term student outcomes.

What Google says, and what comes next

Google has not publicly responded to the letter. The company has pointed to its protections for young users, a claim the senators' final question asks it to substantiate. In May, Google described studies of AI-assisted learning, including a randomised trial of nearly 1,800 students in Sierra Leone in which its Guided Learning tool improved maths assessment results.

Hawley and Blumenthal have worked this ground before: last year the pair introduced the GUARD Act, which would ban AI companions for minors. Pichai's response, due November 2, will show whether Google treats the letter as a disclosure exercise or the opening of a longer legislative fight — and for parents, the immediate question is narrower: whether the AI on their child's school Chromebook can actually be turned off.
